GAEM: Bonds from governments and companies in emerging markets, borrowed in dollars or in local currencies, picked actively. It aims for higher income than developed market bonds, with extra risk from shakier economies and currency swings on the local currency debt.
ZTRE: Bonds from solid, investment grade companies that all come due in about three years, so the lineup rolls over on a tight schedule. Short maturities like these mean smaller price swings when interest rates move, suiting cautious income investors.
MATE: Mostly a big US stock fund at its core, with a trend-following program layered on top that trades futures across world markets. The overlay tries to add returns and soften drops by following market trends, making it more complex than a plain stock fund.
SPBC: Broad US stocks make up about nine tenths of the fund, with the rest in bitcoin funds for a measured dose of crypto. It is for stock investors who want some bitcoin exposure in the same ticker, with crypto adding extra volatility on top.
RBLD: US companies that build, own and run infrastructure, from construction and utility firms to the data and technology names behind modern networks. It leans toward the builders of next generation infrastructure, so it has a growth flavor compared with sleepy utility funds.
JANZ: Options on the S&P 500 designed to cushion part of a market fall over an outcome period that restarts each January, at the cost of some upside. It is actively managed rather than a strict formula, and results depend on when you buy during the period.
INQQ: Indian internet and ecommerce companies: online shopping, food delivery, digital payments and the finance apps behind them. It is a narrow bet on India's digital growth story, so it swings with one country's young, fast-changing online sector.
PBFB: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in February, as the Buffer 20 name suggests. In exchange for that deep cushion, gains are capped, so it trails in strong years.
BAMY: An income-focused fund of funds that gathers high yield bond funds and other paying investments like dividend stocks and preferred shares. The junk bond core reaches for higher income, which brings credit risk: payments look generous because the borrowers are shakier.
MSTQ: Mostly the big Nasdaq growth stocks, held through a large index fund, with the amount adjusted by statistical signals about the market's direction. The tactical overlay can dial exposure up or down, so it will not always be fully invested in stocks.
TCHI: Chinese technology in the broad sense: chip and computer makers, internet platforms, online retailers and battery firms all count. It captures how blurred the tech label is in China, and like all China funds it swings with policy and sentiment toward Beijing.
YLDW: A mix of dividend-paying stocks and interest-bearing bonds, led by big technology, health care and bank names, built to pay income. It targets a calmer ride than a stock-only fund, accepting slower growth in exchange for regular payouts and smaller swings.
TPFC: Fifty large and mid-sized US companies chosen for strong free cash flow, drawn from an index that applies biblically responsible screens. Energy, health care and technology lead the mix, and the values screen sets it apart from ordinary cash flow funds.
GAMR: The leaders of the video game business worldwide: game publishers, console and chip makers, and the platforms where games are played and streamed. It is a pure bet on gaming as entertainment, so it moves with game releases and player spending.
CFIT: Bond funds of many kinds, from Treasury bills to high yield and emerging market debt, selected by a trend-following model. The model shifts toward whatever bond types are rising and steps back from falling ones, so the mix can change a lot over time.
SPXV: The S&P 500 with the entire health care sector left out, so technology takes an even bigger share than usual. It suits investors who already hold health care elsewhere or want less of it, while keeping the rest of the big-company market intact.
ORBX: Companies developing space technology: rocket builders, satellite makers and the firms turning orbit into a business. It is concentrated in a small, young industry, with a few names carrying much of the weight, so news about launches and contracts moves it sharply.
BETZ: Sports betting and online gaming companies from around the world: bookmakers, casino apps and the data and platform firms behind them. It is a narrow wager on gambling going digital and legal in more places, and it swings with regulation and betting volumes.
TYA: It uses futures on US Treasury bonds, with borrowed exposure, to behave like a portfolio of long-term government bonds. Long Treasuries pay steady income and often rise when stocks fall, but their prices drop sharply when interest rates climb.
AUGU: Options on the S&P 500 arranged to absorb the first part of a market loss over a one-year period starting in August, with a 15% buffer built into the design. Upside is uncapped past a starting spread, which is the twist versus ordinary capped buffers.
BEMB: A broad basket of emerging market bonds all borrowed in US dollars, from governments and companies across dozens of countries. Dollar borrowing removes direct currency risk, but the income comes with the credit risk of less settled economies and governments.
IDEC: Options giving exposure to large companies in developed markets outside North America, with a buffer against part of any loss over a period resetting each December. It pairs international diversification with a safety cushion, giving up some gains when overseas markets rally.
IBGM: US Treasury bonds that all come due around the end of 2056, when the fund itself wraps up and pays out. With such long maturities, its price swings a lot when interest rates move, far more than ordinary bond funds.
VBCF: Bonds from large companies, banks, phone and tech firms among them, all chosen to come due around 2032, when the fund winds down. Knowing the end date lets investors line it up with a future spending goal, like a tuition or retirement bill.
CEFZ: An actively managed collection of closed-end funds and other income funds, spanning stocks and bonds around the world. RiverNorth hunts for income funds trading at discounts to their value, so the mix and the risk level shift as bargains appear and disappear.
QTAC: A tactical mix built mainly on futures tied to big US stock indexes, plus leveraged funds, Treasuries and cash for ballast. It shifts with the seasons of the market, aiming to press gains in good times and protect capital when conditions turn rough.
KFEB: Options on a small company index fund designed to absorb part of a loss over a year-long outcome period that resets every February. Gains are capped in return for the cushion, and the options structure means it will not behave exactly like owning small stocks.
EBUF: Options on an emerging markets stock fund, with a buffer meant to absorb roughly the first tenth of losses, resetting every quarter, as the 10 in the name indicates. It tempers the wild swings of emerging markets, at the cost of capped gains.
IGCB: Corporate bonds of many maturities from companies in the US and abroad, including some in emerging markets, picked actively by TCW. It is a core-style bond holding aiming for income with moderate risk, though company debt falls when credit worries grow.
XOCT: Options on the S&P 500 that enhance participation in moderate gains up to a cap, while cushioning part of a decline, over an outcome year resetting each October. The boost on medium-sized rallies is the draw, balanced by limited gains in the biggest years.
TFFI: Bond funds spanning short and longer company debt, preferred shares and emerging market bonds, moved around by a long-term trend-following program. The strategy rides bond trends up or down and can step aside into cash, so it behaves unlike a normal buy-and-hold bond fund.
BCGS: A select, actively managed set of large companies from around the world, led by industrial and technology firms. With only a few dozen holdings, it is a conviction portfolio: each pick counts, so results depend heavily on the managers' judgment.
HWGV: Large companies from around the world bought when their prices look low compared with their underlying worth, in Hotchkis and Wiley's value style. Holdings span software, insurance, health care and industrial names, and the patient approach can lag for stretches before bargains pay off.
KVLE: Dividend-paying US companies selected using Value Line's research rankings, which favor financially steady firms with reliable payouts. Technology and property companies lead the mix, an unusual blend for an income fund, and the rules-based screen aims for dividends that can grow.
XPND: Technology companies in the wider sense: chip and software firms plus the payment networks and platforms whose businesses run on technology. Actively chosen rather than index-bound, it captures tech's reach into finance and media while swinging like a sector fund.
IHY: High yield bonds from companies outside the United States, issued in major currencies like euros and dollars. These junk bonds pay more than safer debt to make up for weaker borrowers, and adding foreign issuers spreads the risk across many economies.
NJNK: Bonds from US companies rated below investment grade, the so-called junk bonds, picked across industries by Columbia's managers. They pay higher income to compensate for weaker borrowers, and prices can drop hard when investors worry about defaults in a downturn.
EMDM: Companies in emerging market countries that qualify as electoral democracies under Freedom House standards, led by Asian chip makers and banks. The democracy filter cuts out giants like China entirely, which sets it apart from ordinary emerging market funds.
FCBD: A core bond portfolio built from other managers' bond funds, covering government, corporate and mortgage debt that is mostly investment grade. Using several outside funds spreads the manager risk, and the core-plus style reaches a little beyond plain vanilla bonds for extra income.
DHSB: It holds a broad US stock fund and layers option spreads on top, a smart buffer design meant to trim losses and add income. The options work means it will trail a plain stock fund in big rallies while aiming for a calmer path overall.
COWS: US companies that both pay dividends and generate strong free cash flow, spread across technology, industrial, energy and financial firms. The double screen aims for income backed by real cash, favoring mature businesses over fast growers with no payouts.
EQRR: Large companies chosen because their share prices have historically tended to rise when interest rates climb, led by energy, technology and financial stocks. It is a hedge for rising rate periods, the mirror image of rate-sensitive funds, so it can lag when rates fall.
CAFG: Small US companies screened for unusually strong free cash flow margins, with technology and health care the biggest groups. It looks for small firms already generating real cash, a quality filter meant to weed out the most fragile small caps.
NIXT: Small and mid-sized US value stocks, built around companies dropped from big stock indexes, which often leaves them temporarily unpopular and cheap. The bet is that yesterday's index castoffs recover, a contrarian corner of the market most funds ignore.
OVS: US small company stocks, held through a broad small cap fund, with an options overlay that sells put options to add income. Small caps bring extra growth potential and extra swings, while the option premiums aim to smooth the ride and pay along the way.
PBAU: Options on the S&P 500 built to absorb the first fifth of a market loss over a one-year period starting in August, in line with the Buffer 20 name. That deep protection costs upside: gains above the buffer design are capped, so it lags in rallies.
TXS: Stocks of companies headquartered in Texas, from energy giants and airlines to health care and technology firms with Texas roots. It is a single-state bet: diversified across industries, but tied to Texas's economy, energy prices and business climate more than a national fund.
MAYM: Options on the S&P 500 aiming for the deepest loss protection the options market allows over a year starting in May, as the Max Buffer name suggests. With protection maxed out, the cap on gains is low, so it barely joins in during strong rallies.
MYCI: Corporate bonds that come due in 2029, from big issuers across industries, gathered into one target-year package. Like a single bond with many borrowers, it suits investors saving toward a 2029 expense who want company debt rather than government debt.
DIVS: Dividend-paying companies from around the world chosen because the manager believes they can keep raising their payouts over the next few years. It favors proven dividend growers over the highest yields, aiming for income that climbs rather than income that is merely large today.
